q: In a relational database, a single row of a table is called a…
why: A tuple is a single row (record). An attribute is a column, a domain is the set of allowed values, and a relation is the whole table.

q: The number of columns (attributes) in a relation is its…
why: Degree = number of columns; cardinality = number of rows. Don't confuse the two.

q: Which key uniquely identifies every row and can never be null?
why: The primary key uniquely identifies each tuple and cannot be null or duplicated. A foreign key references another table's primary key.

q: A foreign key value must match an existing primary key (or be null). This is…
why: Referential integrity ensures relationships stay valid — a foreign key can't point at a non-existent record.

q: One customer can place many orders. This is a…
why: One customer (one) → many orders (many). The primary key of Customer becomes a foreign key in Order.

q: Students can enrol on many courses, and each course has many students. How is this modelled?
why: Many-to-many is resolved with a linking (junction) table holding the two foreign keys, e.g. Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID).

q: Which of these is a desktop (single-file) RDBMS commonly used in this unit?
why: Access is a desktop database — stored locally as a single file. Oracle and MySQL are server databases.

q: MySQL and Oracle are examples of…
why: They are server databases — running centrally and serving many concurrent users over a network.

q: Which SQL keyword retrieves data from a table?
why: SELECT retrieves data. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes.

q: Which SQL statement adds a new record to a table?
why: INSERT INTO adds a new tuple, e.g. INSERT INTO Customer VALUES (...).

q: Repeating groups must be removed so each cell holds a single value. Which normal form is this?
why: First Normal Form (1NF) removes repeating groups — every attribute is atomic.

q: Removing partial-key dependencies (non-key attrs depending on only part of a composite key) achieves…
why: Second Normal Form removes partial dependencies — non-key attributes must depend on the whole primary key.

q: Removing transitive dependencies (non-key attr depending on another non-key attr) achieves…
why: Third Normal Form removes transitive dependencies — non-key attributes depend only on the key.

q: Updating a duplicated phone number in one row but not another causes…
why: Update anomaly — the same data stored in multiple places becomes inconsistent when changed in only one place.

q: Deleting the last student on a course accidentally deletes the course details too. This is…
why: Deletion anomaly — losing related data when removing a record, caused by bad table design.

q: A diagram showing entities, their attributes and relationships is an…
why: An Entity Relationship Diagram models the database design — the core of Aim B.

q: Which ERD shows only entity names and relationships (no attributes)?
why: Conceptual model = high-level (entities + relationships only). Logical adds attributes and keys.

q: A table listing field names, data types, lengths and validation rules is a…
why: The data dictionary documents every field's name, type, length and validation — required design evidence.

q: Which form control lets users pick one value from a drop-down list (often linked to another table)?
why: A combo box restricts input to valid choices, often drawing from a lookup table.

q: An input mask is used to…
why: An input mask guides consistent entry (e.g. postcode LL00 0LL) — part of good form design.

q: A query that prompts the user for a value each time it runs is a…
why: Parameter query asks for input (e.g. 'Enter customer ID') so one query serves many uses.

q: Which query type changes data rather than just displaying it?
why: Action queries (append/update/delete/make-table) modify data. Use with care.

q: A formatted, printable output that can group records and show totals is a…
why: Reports present data for printing — with grouping, calculated fields and conditional formatting.

q: Reviewing a design against 'meeting client requirements, legal/ethical constraints, consistency' is…
why: Self-review checks suitability for user, requirements, legal/ethical constraints and consistency — then refines.

q: Which SQL statement creates a new table?
why: CREATE TABLE defines a new relation with its columns and data types.

q: Enforcing that a child record can't exist without its parent is done through…
why: Defining table relationships with referential integrity ensures child records always have a valid parent.

q: Testing with age = -5, or letters in a number field, uses…
why: Erroneous (invalid) data confirms validation rules correctly reject bad input.

q: Testing with values at the very edge of allowed ranges (0, 120) is…
why: Extreme/boundary data checks the limits of ranges and field lengths — catches overflow and off-by-one bugs.

q: To make a query run faster you should…
options: Select only the columns you need and use efficient joins
why: Selecting specific columns and efficient joins (over slow sub-queries) are key query optimisations.

q: Assessing whether the database meets the client's original requirements is…
why: Fitness for purpose checks the solution against the brief — quality, suitability, legal/ethical constraints.

q: A primary key made from two or more attributes combined is a…
why: Composite key = two+ attributes together uniquely identify a row (e.g. OrderID + ProductID).

q: Combining two relations to produce a single result without duplicates is…
why: Union combines rows from two compatible relations. Intersect returns common rows; join combines on a shared attribute.

q: The wildcard * in a query criterion means…
why: * matches any characters (Access); ? matches a single character. 'S*' finds all values starting with S.

q: A main form containing a related 'child' form showing matching records is…
why: Form + subform shows one parent record with its many children (e.g. an order and its order lines).

q: Checking that links between tables stay valid when records are added/deleted is…
why: Referential integrity testing verifies relationships hold — no orphans, blocked deletes of parents with children.

q: The first step when scoping a database solution to a brief is…
why: Preliminary scoping starts with the problem to be solved and technical requirements, then research existing databases.

q: Every table must have a primary key that is never null or duplicated. This is…
why: Entity integrity guarantees each row is uniquely identifiable via its primary key.

q: Storing images directly inside a table can bloat the file. A better approach is…
options: Store image paths, not the images themselves
why: Storing paths/references keeps the database small and fast — part of optimising data storage.

q: Building and testing a basic working version early, then refining it, is…
why: Prototyping builds an early version to test ideas and get feedback before full development.

q: Which document lists the steps and timescales for building the database?
why: The implementation plan sets out steps and timescales — part of the design specification.
